#FITSPIRATION

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
#Fitspiration - a health revolution pushing the pursuit of perfection fuelled by compulisve exercise and restrictive eating – is this new health drive becoming toxic.

Summary:
While the health revolution is taking the world by storm – it has the potential to go toxic. Driven by a perception of perfection peddled by so-called social media gurus people are becoming fixated on exercise and healthy eating. But, too much of a good thing is never good – and can have serious damaging effects.

We explore the smoke & mirrors behind #fitspiration and ask just good #cleaneating really is?

THE MORAL OF THE STORY – EVERYTHING WITH MODERATION AND BALANCE! REALISE THAT WE ARE ALL UNIQUE AND THE PERSUIT OF PERFECTION SHOULD BE INDIVIDUALISED AND NOT ONE SIZE FITS ALL!

Further information:
WHAT ARE TALKING ABOUT:
#CleanEating - where people avoid processed foods, sugar and gluten in favour of fruit, vegetables and wholegrains - has been spearheaded by numerous foodies with large social media followings.
#fitspiration = Fit + inspiration. A healthier alternative to thinspiration, fitspiration is using examples of good fitness (people, photographs, skinny jeans, etc) as inspiration to attain a fitness goal/ motivation for someone to sustain or improve health and fitness.

Orthorexia – while it hasn’t been classified as an eating disorder and is still in it’s infancy as a decease – specialist are talking about it – it’s an obsession to eat a healthy diet leading to aniexity and stress.
BUT WHERE IS THE MOTIVATION COMING FROM?
If you’ve ever scrolled through your instagram feed looking for work out inspiration or a new twist to healthy meal options – you don’t have to search too far – STRONG IS THE NEW SKINNY!

There are countless bloggers posting fitness mantras with millions of followers – these people have being the rock stars of social media. But are these so-called healthy eating gurus peddling facts and science or just what ever goes to boost likes and followers?

Instagram Health Bloggers are now more influential than celebrities but are these online fitness mantras being peddled as #FITSPIRATION really sending out the right message? With social media, anyone can share dietary advice online..

Worryingly, many of the most popular fitness bloggers have not formal fitness or nutritional training yet some advocate diets that cut out large food groups. This can have a devastating impact on the people who follow the militant diets they advocate.

The damaging results of people offering advice through blogs who are not qualified to do so, with serious conditions, such as osteoprorosis, nutritional deficiencies, muscle wastage and joint damage arising form ingrained misinformation.

Generalised advice is often inadequate.

While there is no harm in seeking advice and motivation – online – it can often have opposite effect. – it can deflate you, rock your confidence and play havoc with your body image. These social media profiles don’t promote body love, but rather body fear and pressure.
“Fitspiration” promotes that every other body type should not be celebrated.

If these images and messages categorized as “fitness inspiration” actually inspire body shame – you feel ashamed of the beauty ideals you cannot reach and want to hide or judge your body or covet other women’s bodies – then these messages are not inspirational at all. They trigger you to feel anxiety, hopelessness, and ask you to resort to extremes to get somewhere largely unattainable for healthy people, which does not discount that some people may be able to attain that ideal, but most cannot.
Three main values that are instilled results from fitspiration are control, perfection, and success. To some, these values may seem positive, but more often than not, they can destroy a person’s life. Focusing on only those things allows other parts of a person’s life to fall away.
There is evidence that since the fitspiration movement began, the amount of eating disorder cases has increased significantly.
But too much of a good thing can be BAD – becoming obsessed with diet and fitness can take your health revolution to a dangerous restrictive level fuelling a quest / desire for perfection. Orthorexia is categorised as an obsession with healthy eating. While orthorexia is not clinically recognised – cases are soring at an alarming rate as health bloggers champion gluten-free, sugar-free and raw-food diets. It is the compulsion to eat a healthy diet.

Symptoms include constantly worrying about food, and sufferers feel guilt or self-loathing when they stray from their diet. They feel in control when they are on diet; they tend to wear healthy eating like a badge of honour. They place themselves on a nutritional pedestal and they wonder how others can possible eat other food. Food becomes a constant obsession.

THE INTERVIEWS

SIHLE NKOSI – FITNESS FANATIC
Sihle is a 31 year old financial adviser. She exercises 6 -7 days a week, plays netball and cricket. She follows fitness blogs and posts on social media and while she says she is happy – she is striving towards an ideal body image that is strong and toned – one that is not always attainable. She is beautiful but no athlete – she is the example of how even with excessive exercise – perfection is not the same for everyone because of genetics and body make up.

ULRIKE BORGENHEIM – CLEANEATING ENTHUSIAST
Ulrike suffered from anorexia, but has replaced that eating disorder with a new one – she is fixated on healthy eating – STRONG is the new skinny. She explains how her need to only eat whole foods makes her anxious and puts a great deal of stress on her. She is reluctant to be classified as orthorexic – but acknowledges her obessession.

PROF CHRISTOPHER SZABO – PSYCHIATRIST
Prof Szabo explains that psychological impacts of compulsive exercise and a fixation with clean eating. He talks about balance and acceptance and the risks that any obsessive behaviour plays on a persons emotional wellbeing.

JESSICA SEPEL
Jessica is an Australian qualified nutritionist and health author – she has gone full circle with the pursuit of perfection and has come to a place of acceptance – advocating the value of balance in life while reflecting on the destructiveness of behaviour related to the health revolution and when it can become toxic.

TBOGO XX – FITNESS SPECIALIST
TBOGO is a 30 year old personal trainer – she is outspoken about the effects of social media and the ideas that are being peddled by unqualified health gurus. She will talk about how we are all different and that fitness means different things for people – everyone can’t have a six pack – but can still be fit. We will do a demonstration of an instagram before and after transformation – how it’s all smoke and mirrors.

IAN CRAIG
Ian is a UK born exercise physiologist, nutritional therapist, NLP practitioner and a lifestyle coach – he has studied internationally and has three degrees in the field.
Ian specialises in functional nutrition, a fast-evolving discipline that considers both the health and performance of an individual from an integrative health perspective. He personalises exercise and nutrition strategies according to the individual attributes and lifestyles of his clients. He treats people with obsessive and excessive behaviours when it comes to exercise and eating.

Press Release:


Fitspiration
Fuelled by compulsive exercise and restrictive eating, Fitspiration is the health revolution that’s pushing the pursuit of perfection to its
limits. From strange dieting regimes, to extreme body transformations, there’s almost nothing you can’t find on social media. But in the quest for
the perfect body, is this new health drive becoming toxic? Carte Blanche explores this growing trend.

Script:


FITSPIRATION

VO: Billions of people around the world are hooked on Social Media – it’s how we connect, communicate and now even the inspiration for health and fitness movements with hashtags #Fitspiration…#Fitness…and #CleanEating…. dominating platforms like Instagram.

SIHLE: first thing when I wake up on social media – checking out food / checking out people with beautiful bodies
LINDO: every time I look at them – I want to go to the gym – do more hours – push more weights….

VO: Getting in shape has never been more popular.

Globally, there are 180 000 fitness clubs, turning over $84 billion in blood, sweat and tears from 145 million members every year.

SIHLE NKOSI – 31 year old is a FINANCIAL ADVISOR - she TRAINS 6 times a week.

SIHLE: I don’t want to be thin, I want to be toned, I want to be fit.

VO: LINDO SEETI is a 21 year old student, he trains 3 hours a day, 6 times a week.

LINDO: basically the goal is to be buff //just better than what I am right now…

VO: With the rise of obesity and a growing fixation on health – the world is primed for a revolution.

LINK: It’s a health revolution…. Strong is the new skinny in the pursuit of perfection, but what happens when a lifestyle choice turns toxic.

TEBOGO: When it comes to social media – people want to have the perception that they can become what they are looking at

VO: Personal Trainer, Tebogo Dikgale says it impacts negatively on the industry – gyms are swamped by people pushing themselves excessively hard and training compulsively.

The reality is there is no miracle plan that delivers fitness for everyone says nutritional specialist and exercise physiologist - Ian Craig – it’s a unique integrated process.

IAN: Everyone is totally genetically individual //one of the most damaging result of following wrong regime is over training, burn out, adrenal fatigue, chronic fatigue, auto immune conditions

VO: In this pursuit of perceived perfection people are becoming fixated on exercise and healthy eating – a growing trend Ian’s noticed in his practice.

IAN: biggest thing I worry about is the controlled behaviour – restricts the mind, restricts the social interaction

VO: Lindo has been gymming since the age of 14 – he says exercise puts him on a high.

LINDO: when not school – gym is all I think about – other kids think about drinks and smoking – I want to go to gym… that’s where I want to be…
DEVI: are you too hard on yourself sometimes?
LINDO: I am, but I see it as a good thing….

VO: BUT IS IT? When does too much of a good thing become bad? Psychiatrist, Prof Christopher Szabo points out that any kind of compulsive behaviour could take a toll on emotional wellbeing.

SZABO: When you aspire to something that is unrealistic you may adopt habits that set you up for an eating disorder.//so this pursuit of health could ultimately lead to development of pathology.

VO: It’s called Orthorexia – it has NOT been classified as a disorder – but is recognised internationally as a fixation on righteous eating – focussed only on healthy and organic foods.

Australian nutritionist and health author Jessica Sepel says she has been down this destructive road as a teenager.

JESSICA: //fixated on eating healthy all the time and a lot of fear, anxiety and guilt around not eating healthy food.

VO: She says her obsession impacted on every aspect of her life.

JESSICA: I found have family gatherings stressful,// I would feel judged, in social environment with friends that were balanced // all different social environments were difficult for me because I was restrictive //

VO: But being excessively restrictive about any food will lead to some level of deprivation says Ian.

IAN: the most unhealthy clients, I have seen are not the ones eating the worse, are the ones supposedly eating the best // they’re the ones with a long list of health complaints. INT3 M4

JESSICA: //I wasn’t feeling good, my mood was low, I wasn’t sleeping well, my cortisol levels were sky high, my hair was breaking, my skin was breaking out – I didn’t feel good about myself.

VO: While Jessica was studying her bachelor of health, she realised the negative impact her actions were having on her body and she decided that it was time for change.

JESSICA: I made a commitment to give up dieting for life. Working on being kinder to myself when it came to food, I was including all the food groups – I started to embrace balance and the results were incredible

VO: While Jessica shares her health mantra based on her experience and qualifications – there are unqualified people flooding the online health revolution.

SZABO: you have an individual that has set up as an expert // on what basis does this person speak with this kind of authority – this could just be the confidence of the encyclous

VO: Sihle Nkosi is a self-proclaimed fitness freak - she turns to social media for everything from workouts to nutrition inspiration.

SIHLE: // social media tells us what to do and how. // I have a picture, instructions - I can download from instagram.

VO: While Sihle says she is happy, she is still working towards an ideal body image.

SIHLE: I feel like I have some work to do.

VO: While techonology gives everyone access to a range of fitness and health tools, it also promotes an unhealthy mentality of instant gratification often driven by unrealistic goals says TEBOGO.

TEBOGO: Clients on social media, // Clients complain – training for a month, not losing weight.

LINK: Social Media health gurus are even more influential than celebrities - peddling exercise regimes and eating plans, promising transformation but some say all they are delivering anxiety and body shame.

IAN: You get genetic individuality – square person tries to fit themselves in round pen – become disillusioned…. INT1 M3

VO: The disillusion is fuelled by social media. Recently the 30 second transformation hashtag flooded Instagram with images of fake before and after pics.

DEVI: Show me how to create the smoke and mirrors?
TEBOGO: I’m going to show you how we are going to take the gorgeous woman into ripped in 30 seconds
DEVI: 30 seconds!

VO: Tebogo instructed her how to pose – tummy in, shoulders back.

This is the before pic on the left, and the after pic on the right.

DEVI: completely different M31 // It’s just about pulling a few smart moves
TEBOGO: this is not going to take you three months, six months, it’s going to take a few minutes.

DEVI: So how do we get the booty shot right?
TEBOGO: that is so easy…
TEBOGO: it can accentuated by her positioning.

VO: And just like that she’s gone from normal to bootilicious.

SZABO: // what comes back to what is idealised and what is real – we need to be realistic about what we are and who we are – where we try to push our body where it doesn’t want to go we are going to have problems. INT1 M17

JESSICA: //comparison is so toxic, we need to create our own definition of what beautiful is. INT1 M23




PROMOS
PROMO 1
VO: We explore the smoke & mirrors behind the online health revolution?

SZABO: When you aspire to something that is unrealistic you may adopt habits that set you up for problems.

PROMO 2
VO: A health revolution or a dangerous pursuit for perfection? Is compulsive exercise and restrictive eating becoming toxic.

IAN: biggest thing I worry about is the controlled behaviour – restricts the mind, restricts the social interaction INT3 M4

PROMO 3
VO: When it comes to the online health revolution – how realistic is the pursuit of pefection?

JESSICA: //comparison is so toxic, we need to create our own definition of what beautiful is. INT1 M23

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): #Fitspiration - a health revolution pushing the pursuit of perfection fuelled by compulisve exercise and restrictive eating – is this new health drive becoming toxic.
metadata.Summary: While the health revolution is taking the world by storm – it has the potential to go toxic. Driven by a perception of perfection peddled by so-called social media gurus people are becoming fixated on exercise and healthy eating. But, too much of a good thing is never good – and can have serious damaging effects. We explore the smoke & mirrors behind #fitspiration and ask just good #cleaneating really is? THE MORAL OF THE STORY – EVERYTHING WITH MODERATION AND BALANCE! REALISE THAT WE ARE ALL UNIQUE AND THE PERSUIT OF PERFECTION SHOULD BE INDIVIDUALISED AND NOT ONE SIZE FITS ALL!
metadata.Further information: WHAT ARE TALKING ABOUT: #CleanEating - where people avoid processed foods, sugar and gluten in favour of fruit, vegetables and wholegrains - has been spearheaded by numerous foodies with large social media followings. #fitspiration = Fit + inspiration. A healthier alternative to thinspiration, fitspiration is using examples of good fitness (people, photographs, skinny jeans, etc) as inspiration to attain a fitness goal/ motivation for someone to sustain or improve health and fitness. Orthorexia – while it hasn’t been classified as an eating disorder and is still in it’s infancy as a decease – specialist are talking about it – it’s an obsession to eat a healthy diet leading to aniexity and stress. BUT WHERE IS THE MOTIVATION COMING FROM? If you’ve ever scrolled through your instagram feed looking for work out inspiration or a new twist to healthy meal options – you don’t have to search too far – STRONG IS THE NEW SKINNY! There are countless bloggers posting fitness mantras with millions of followers – these people have being the rock stars of social media. But are these so-called healthy eating gurus peddling facts and science or just what ever goes to boost likes and followers? Instagram Health Bloggers are now more influential than celebrities but are these online fitness mantras being peddled as #FITSPIRATION really sending out the right message? With social media, anyone can share dietary advice online.. Worryingly, many of the most popular fitness bloggers have not formal fitness or nutritional training yet some advocate diets that cut out large food groups. This can have a devastating impact on the people who follow the militant diets they advocate. The damaging results of people offering advice through blogs who are not qualified to do so, with serious conditions, such as osteoprorosis, nutritional deficiencies, muscle wastage and joint damage arising form ingrained misinformation. Generalised advice is often inadequate. While there is no harm in seeking advice and motivation – online – it can often have opposite effect. – it can deflate you, rock your confidence and play havoc with your body image. These social media profiles don’t promote body love, but rather body fear and pressure. “Fitspiration” promotes that every other body type should not be celebrated. If these images and messages categorized as “fitness inspiration” actually inspire body shame – you feel ashamed of the beauty ideals you cannot reach and want to hide or judge your body or covet other women’s bodies – then these messages are not inspirational at all. They trigger you to feel anxiety, hopelessness, and ask you to resort to extremes to get somewhere largely unattainable for healthy people, which does not discount that some people may be able to attain that ideal, but most cannot. Three main values that are instilled results from fitspiration are control, perfection, and success. To some, these values may seem positive, but more often than not, they can destroy a person’s life. Focusing on only those things allows other parts of a person’s life to fall away. There is evidence that since the fitspiration movement began, the amount of eating disorder cases has increased significantly. But too much of a good thing can be BAD – becoming obsessed with diet and fitness can take your health revolution to a dangerous restrictive level fuelling a quest / desire for perfection. Orthorexia is categorised as an obsession with healthy eating. While orthorexia is not clinically recognised – cases are soring at an alarming rate as health bloggers champion gluten-free, sugar-free and raw-food diets. It is the compulsion to eat a healthy diet. Symptoms include constantly worrying about food, and sufferers feel guilt or self-loathing when they stray from their diet. They feel in control when they are on diet; they tend to wear healthy eating like a badge of honour. They place themselves on a nutritional pedestal and they wonder how others can possible eat other food. Food becomes a constant obsession. THE INTERVIEWS SIHLE NKOSI – FITNESS FANATIC Sihle is a 31 year old financial adviser. She exercises 6 -7 days a week, plays netball and cricket. She follows fitness blogs and posts on social media and while she says she is happy – she is striving towards an ideal body image that is strong and toned – one that is not always attainable. She is beautiful but no athlete – she is the example of how even with excessive exercise – perfection is not the same for everyone because of genetics and body make up. ULRIKE BORGENHEIM – CLEANEATING ENTHUSIAST Ulrike suffered from anorexia, but has replaced that eating disorder with a new one – she is fixated on healthy eating – STRONG is the new skinny. She explains how her need to only eat whole foods makes her anxious and puts a great deal of stress on her. She is reluctant to be classified as orthorexic – but acknowledges her obessession. PROF CHRISTOPHER SZABO – PSYCHIATRIST Prof Szabo explains that psychological impacts of compulsive exercise and a fixation with clean eating. He talks about balance and acceptance and the risks that any obsessive behaviour plays on a persons emotional wellbeing. JESSICA SEPEL Jessica is an Australian qualified nutritionist and health author – she has gone full circle with the pursuit of perfection and has come to a place of acceptance – advocating the value of balance in life while reflecting on the destructiveness of behaviour related to the health revolution and when it can become toxic. TBOGO XX – FITNESS SPECIALIST TBOGO is a 30 year old personal trainer – she is outspoken about the effects of social media and the ideas that are being peddled by unqualified health gurus. She will talk about how we are all different and that fitness means different things for people – everyone can’t have a six pack – but can still be fit. We will do a demonstration of an instagram before and after transformation – how it’s all smoke and mirrors. IAN CRAIG Ian is a UK born exercise physiologist, nutritional therapist, NLP practitioner and a lifestyle coach – he has studied internationally and has three degrees in the field. Ian specialises in functional nutrition, a fast-evolving discipline that considers both the health and performance of an individual from an integrative health perspective. He personalises exercise and nutrition strategies according to the individual attributes and lifestyles of his clients. He treats people with obsessive and excessive behaviours when it comes to exercise and eating.
